This threefold austerity practised by steadfast men, with great Shraddhâ, desiring no fruit, is said to be Sâttvika.
That austerity which is practised with the object of gaining welcome, honour and worship, and with ostentation, is here said to be Râjasika, unstable and transitory.
That austerity which is practised out of a foolish notion, with self-torture or for the purpose of wining another, is declared to be Tâmasika.
To give is right, gift given with this idea, to one who does no service in return, in a fit place and to a worthy person, that gift is held to be Sâttvika.
And what is given with a view to receiving in return, or looking for the fruit, or again reluctantly, that gift is held to be Râjasika.
The gift that is given at the wrong place or time, to unworthy persons, without regard or with disdain, that is declared to be Tâmasika.
"Om, Tat, Sat": this has been declared to be the triple designation of Brahman. By that were made of old the Brâhmanas, the Vedas and the Yajnas.
Therefore, uttering 'Om,' are the acts of sacrifice, gift and austerity as enjoined in the ordinances, always begun by the followers of the Vedas.
Uttering Tat, without aiming at fruits, are the various acts of Yajna, austerity and gift performed by the seekers of Moksha.
The word Sat is used in the sense of reality and of goodness; and so also, Pârtha, the word Sat is used in the sense of an auspicious act.
Steadiness in Yajna, austerity and gift is also called 'Sat': as also action in connection with these (or, action for the sake of the Lord) is called Sat.
Whatever is sacrificed, given or performed, and whatever austerity is practised without Shraddhâ, it is called Asat, O Pârtha; it is naught here or hereafter.
I desire to know severally, O mighty-armed, the truth of Sannyâsa, O Hrishikesha, as also of Tyâga, O slayer of Keshi.
The renunciation of Kâmya actions, the sages understand as. Sannyâsa: the wise declare the abandonment of the fruits of all works as Tyâga.
Some philosophers declare that all action should be relinquished as an evil, whilst others (say) that the work of Yajna, gift and austerity should not be relinquished.
Hear from Me the final truth about relinquishment, O best of the Bhâratas. For relinquishment has been declared to be of three kinds, O tiger among men.
The work of Yajna, gift and austerity should not be relinquished, but it should indeed be performed; (for) Yajna, gift and austerity are purifying to the wise.
But even these works, O Pârtha, should be performed, leaving attachment and the fruits;—such is My best and certain conviction.
But the renunciation of obligatory action is not proper. Abandonment of the same from delusion is declared to be Tâmasika.
He who from fear of bodily trouble relinquishes action, because it is painful, thus performing a Râjasika relinquishment, he obtains not the fruit thereof.
When obligatory work is performed, O Arjuna, only because it ought to be done, leaving attachment and fruit, such relinquishment is regarded as Sâttvika.
The relinquisher endued with Sattva and a steady understanding and with his doubts dispelled, hates not a disagreeable work nor is attached to an agreeable one.
Actions cannot be entirely relinquished by an embodied being, but he who relinquishes the fruits of action is called a relinquisher.
The threefold fruit of action—disagreeable, agreeable and mixed,—accrues to non-relinquishers after death, but never to relinquishers.
Learn from Me, O mighty-armed, these five causes for the accomplishment of all works as declared in the wisdom which is the end of all action:
The body, the agent, the various senses, the different functions of a manifold kind, and the presiding divinity, the fifth of these;
Whatever action a man performs by his body, speech and mind—whether right or the reverse—these five are its causes.
Such being the case, he who through a non-purified understanding looks upon his Self, the Absolute, as the agent, he of perverted mind sees not.
He who is free from the notion of egoism, whose intelligence is not affected (by good or evil), though he kills these people, he kills not, nor is bound (by the action);
concept: Freedom from ego and karmic bondage

text: Knowledge, the known and the knower form the threefold cause of action. The instrument, the object and the agent are the threefold basis of action.
Knowledge, action and agent are declared in the Sânkhya philosophy to be
That by which the one indestructible Substance is seen in all beings, inseparate in the separated, know that knowledge to be Sâttvika.
But that knowledge which sees in all beings various entities of distinct kinds as different from one another, know thou that knowledge as Râjasika.
Whilst that which is confined to one single effect as if it were the whole, without reason, without foundation in truth, and trivial,—that is declared to be Tâmasika.
An ordained action done without love or hatred by one not desirous of the fruit and free from attachment, is declared to be Sâttvika.
But the action which is performed desiring desires, or with self-conceit and with much effort, is declared to be Râjasika.
That action is declared to be Tâmasika which is undertaken through delusion, without heed to the consequence, loss (of power and wealth), injury (to others) and (one's own) ability.
An agent who is free from attachment, non-egotistic, endued with fortitude and enthusiasm and unaffected in success or failure, is called Sâttvika.
He who is passionate, desirous of the fruits of action, greedy, malignant, impure, easily elated or dejected, such an agent is called Râjasika.
Unsteady, vulgar, arrogant, dishonest, malicious, indolent, desponding and procrastinating, such an agent is called Tâmasika.
Hear thou the triple distinction of intellect and fortitude, according to the Gunas, as I declare them exhaustively and severally, O Dhananjaya.
That which knows the paths of work and renunciation, right and wrong action, fear and fearlessness, bondage and liberation, that intellect, O Pârtha, is Sâttvika.
concept: Sattvika intellect distinguishes right/wrong, fear/fearlessness, bondage/liberation

text: That which has a distorted apprehension of Dharma and its opposite and also of right action and its opposite, that intellect, O Pârtha, is Râjasika.
concept: Rajasic intellect has distorted understanding of Dharma and action

text: That which enveloped in darkness regards Adharma as Dharma and views all things in a perverted light, that intellect, O Pârtha, is Tâmasika.
concept: Tamasic intellect mistakes Adharma for Dharma

text: The fortitude by which the functions of the mind, the Prâna and the senses, O Pârtha, are regulated, that fortitude, unswerving through Yoga, is Sâttvika.
concept: Sattvika fortitude regulates mind, life-force and senses through Yoga

text: But the fortitude by which one regulates (one's mind) to Dharma, desire and wealth, desirous of the fruit of each from attachment, that fortitude, O Pârtha, is Râjasika.
concept: Rajasic fortitude pursues Dharma, desire and wealth for their fruits

text: That by which a stupid man does not give up sleep, fear, grief, despondency and also overweening conceit, that fortitude, O Pârtha, is Tâmasika.
concept: Tamasic fortitude remains attached to sleep, fear, grief and delusion

text: And now hear from Me, O bull of the Bhâratas, of the threefold happiness. That happiness which one learns to enjoy by habit, and by which one comes to the end of pain;
concept: Threefold nature of happiness and its relationship to overcoming pain

text: That which is like poison at first, but like nectar at the end; that happiness is declared to be Sâttvika, born of the translucence of intellect due to Self-realisation.
concept: Sattvika happiness begins difficult but ends in lasting joy through Self-realisation

text: That which arises from the contact of object with sense, at first like nectar, but at the end like poison, that happiness is declared to be Râjasika.
concept: Rajasic happiness begins pleasurable but ends in suffering

text: That happiness which begins and results in self-delusion arising from sleep, indolence and miscomprehension, that is declared to be Tâmasika.
concept: Tamasic happiness arises from sleep, indolence and delusion

text: There is no entity on earth, or again in heaven among the Devas, that is devoid of these three Gunas, born of Prakriti.
concept: All beings are influenced by the three Gunas of Prakriti

text: Of Brâhmanas and Kshatriyas and Vaishyas, as also of Sudras, O scorcher of foes, the duties are distributed according to the Gunas born of their own nature.
concept: Duties are distributed according to nature and the Gunas

text: The control of the mind and the senses, austerity, purity, forbearance, and also uprightness, knowledge, realisation, belief in a hereafter,—these are the duties of the Brâhmanas, born of (their own) nature.
concept: Duties and qualities associated with Brahmanas

text: Prowess, boldness, fortitude, dexterity, and also not flying from battle, generosity and sovereignty are the duties of the Kshatriyas, born of (their own) nature.
concept: Duties and qualities associated with Kshatriyas

text: Agriculture, cattle-rearing and trade are the duties of the Vaishyas, born of (their own) nature; and action consisting of service is the duty of the Sudras, born of (their own) nature.
concept: Duties associated with Vaishyas and Sudras

text: Devoted each to his own duty, man attains the highest perfection. How engaged in his own duty, he attains perfection, that hear.
concept: Performing one's own duty leads toward perfection

text: From whom is the evolution of all beings, by whom all this is pervaded, worshipping Him with his own duty, a man attains perfection.
concept: Worship through one's own duty leads to perfection

text: Better is one's own Dharma, (though) imperfect, than the Dharma of another well-performed. He who does the duty ordained by his own nature incurs no evil.
concept: One's own Dharma is preferable to another's Dharma

text: One should not relinquish, O son of Kunti, the duty to which one is born, though it is attended with evil; for, all undertakings are enveloped by evil, as fire by smoke.
concept: One should not abandon one's inherent duty despite imperfections

text: He whose intellect is unattached everywhere, who has subdued his heart, whose desires have fled, he attains by renunciation to the supreme perfection, consisting of freedom from action.
concept: Renunciation, detachment and mastery lead to supreme perfection

text: Learn from Me in brief, O son of Kunti, how reaching such perfection, he attains to Brahman, that supreme consummation of knowledge.
concept: Krishna explains the path from perfection to Brahman

text: Endued with a pure intellect, subduing the body and the senses with fortitude, relinquishing sound and such other sense-objects, abandoning attraction and hatred;
concept: Pure intellect, sense restraint and freedom from attraction and hatred

text: Resorting to a sequestered spot, eating but little, body, speech and mind
concept: Seclusion, moderation and disciplined body, speech and mind

text: Forsaking egoism, power, pride, lust, wrath and property, freed from the notion of "mine," and tranquil, he is fit for becoming Brahman.
concept: Abandoning ego, pride, desire, anger and possessiveness leads toward Brahman

text: Brahman-become, tranquil-minded, he neither grieves nor desires; the same to all beings, he attains to supreme devotion unto Me.
concept: Brahman-realised person becomes tranquil, desireless and equal toward all beings

text: By devotion he knows Me in
concept: Devotion enables knowledge of Krishna's true nature

text: Even doing all actions always, taking refuge in Me,—by My grace he attains to the eternal, immutable State.
concept: Taking refuge in Krishna while acting leads to the eternal state

text: Resigning mentally all deeds to Me, having Me as the highest goal, resorting to Buddhi-Yoga do thou ever fix thy mind on Me.
concept: Dedicate actions to Krishna and maintain the mind on Him

text: Fixing thy mind on Me, thou shalt, by My grace, overcome all obstacles; but if from self-conceit thou wilt not hear Me, thou shalt perish.
concept: Fixing the mind on Krishna helps overcome obstacles

text: If filled with self-conceit thou thinkest, "I will not fight," vain is this thy resolve; thy Prakriti will constrain thee.
concept: Ego-driven refusal to act is overcome by one's inherent nature

text: Fettered, O son of Kunti, by thy own Karma, born of thy own nature, what thou, from delusion, desirest not to do, thou shalt have to do in spite of thyself.
concept: One is compelled to act according to one's nature and Karma

text: The Lord, O Arjuna, dwells in the hearts of all beings, causing all beings, by His Mâyâ, to revolve, (as if) mounted on a machine.
concept: The Lord dwells in all beings and governs their movement through Maya

text: Take refuge in Him with all thy heart, O Bhârata; by His grace shalt thou
concept: Take complete refuge in the Lord for His grace and highest state

text: Thus has wisdom more profound than all profundities, been declared to. thee by Me; reflecting over it fully, act as thou likest.
concept: Reflect deeply on the teaching and choose one's course of action

text: Hear thou again My supreme word, the profoundest of all; because thou art dearly beloved of Me, therefore will I speak what is good to thee.
concept: Krishna gives His highest teaching out of love for Arjuna

text: Occupy thy mind with Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, bow down to Me. Thou shalt reach Myself; truly do I promise unto thee, (for) thou art dear to Me.
concept: Remember, worship and surrender to Krishna to attain Him

text: Relinquishing all Dharmas take
concept: Abandon all limited Dharmas and surrender completely to Krishna

text: This is never to be spoken by thee to one who is devoid of austerities or devotion, nor to one who does not render service, nor to one who cavils at Me.
concept: The profound teaching should not be given to those lacking devotion or discipline

text: He who with supreme devotion to Me will teach this deeply profound philosophy to My devotees, shall doubtless come to Me alone.
concept: Teaching this wisdom to devoted people is considered supreme service

text: Nor among men is there any who does dearer service to Me, nor shall there be another on earth dearer to Me, than he.
concept: One who teaches the divine teaching is especially dear to Krishna

text: And he who will study this sacred dialogue of ours, by him shall I have been worshipped by the Yajna of knowledge; such is My conviction.
concept: Studying the dialogue is regarded as worship through knowledge

text: And even that man who hears this, full of Shraddhâ and free from malice, he too, liberated, shall attain to the happy worlds of those of righteous deeds.
concept: Hearing the teaching with faith and without malice leads to liberation

text: Has this been heard by thee, Pârtha, with an attentive mind? Has the delusion of thy ignorance been destroyed, O Dhananjaya?
concept: Krishna asks whether Arjuna's delusion and ignorance have been destroyed

text: Destroyed is my delusion, and I have gained my memory through Thy grace, O Achyuta. I am firm; my doubts are gone. I will do Thy word.
concept: Arjuna declares that his delusion and doubts are gone and he will follow Krishna's instruction

text: Thus have I heard this wonderful dialogue between Vâsudeva and the high-souled Pârtha, causing my hair to stand on end.
concept: Sanjaya recounts hearing the profound dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna

text: Through the grace of Vyâsa have I heard this supreme and most profound Yoga, direct from Krishna, the Lord of Yoga, Himself declaring it.
concept: Sanjaya describes hearing the Yoga directly through Vyasa's grace

text: O King, as I remember and remember this wonderful and holy dialogue between Keshava and Arjuna, I rejoice again and again.
concept: Sanjaya remembers the sacred dialogue and experiences repeated joy

text: And as I remember and remember that most wonderful Form of Hari, great is my wonder, O King; and I rejoice again and again.
concept: Sanjaya remembers Krishna's divine form with wonder and joy

text: Wherever is Krishna, the Lord of Yoga, wherever is Pârtha, the wielder of the bow, there are prosperity, victory, expansion, and sound policy: such is my conviction.
concept: Wherever Krishna and Arjuna stand together, prosperity, victory and righteous policy prevail

text: ALL this, whatsoever moves on earth, is to be hidden in the Lord (the Self). When thou hast surrendered all this, then thou mayest enjoy. Do not covet the wealth of any man!
Though a man may wish to live a hundred years, performing works, it will be thus with him; but not in any other way: work will thus not cling to a man.

There are the worlds of the Asuras 1 covered with blind darkness. Those who have destroyed their self (who perform works, without having arrived at a knowledge of the true Self ), go after death to those worlds.
concept: Consequences of ignorance of the Self

text: That one (the Self), though never stirring, is swifter than thought. The Devas (senses) never reached it, it walked 2 before them. Though standing still, it overtakes the others who are running. Mâtarisvan (the wind, the moving spirit) bestows powers 3 on it.
concept: Nature of the Self as beyond thought and senses

text: It stirs and it stirs not; it is far, and likewise near 1 . It is inside of all this, and it is outside of all this.
concept: Self is both moving and unmoving, near and far

text: And he who beholds all beings in the Self, and the Self in all beings, he never turns away from it 2 .
concept: Seeing the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self

text: When to a man who understands, the Self has become all things, what sorrow, what trouble can there be to him who once beheld that unity?
He 3 (the Self) encircled all, bright, incorporeal, scatheless, without muscles, pure, untouched by evil; a seer, wise, omnipresent, self-existent, he disposed all things rightly for eternal years.
All who worship what is not real knowledge (good works), enter into blind darkness: those who delight in real knowledge, enter, as it were, into greater darkness.
concept: Limits and consequences of incomplete knowledge

text: One thing, they say, is obtained from real knowledge; another, they say, from what is not knowledge. Thus we have heard from the wise who taught us this 4 .
He who knows at the same time both knowledge and not-knowledge, overcomes death through not-knowledge, and obtains immortality through knowledge.
All who worship what is not the true cause,
concept: Worship of an improper or false cause

text: One thing, they say, is obtained from (knowledge of) the cause; another, they say, from (knowledge of) what is not the cause. Thus we have heard from the wise who taught us this.
concept: Knowledge of the cause and non-cause

text: He who knows at the same time both the cause and the destruction (the perishable body), overcomes death by destruction (the perishable body), and obtains immortality through (knowledge of ) the true cause.
concept: Understanding the cause and the perishable body

text: The door of the True is covered with a golden disk 1 . Open that, O Pûshan, that we may see the nature of the True 2 .
O Pûshan, only seer, Yama (judge), Sûrya (sun), son of Pra g âpati, spread thy rays and gather them! The light which is thy fairest form, I see it. I am what He is (viz. the person in the sun) 3 .
concept: Identification of the Self with the Supreme

text: Breath 4 to air, and to the immortal! Then this my body ends in ashes. Om! Mind, remember! Remember thy deeds! Mind, remember! Remember thy deeds 5 !
concept: Remembering one's actions and preparing for death

text: Agni, lead us on to wealth (beatitude) by a good path, thou, O God, who knowest all things!
concept: Seeking divine guidance toward the good

text: Those observers of religious rites that perform only the worship of the sacred fire, and oblations to sages, to ancestors,
concept: Religious rites and sacred fire worship

text: VÂ G A S RAVASA 1 , desirous (of heavenly rewards), surrendered (at a sacrifice) all that he possessed. He had a son of the name of Na k iketas.
concept: Vajashravasa performs a sacrifice and gives away his possessions

text: When the (promised) presents were being given (to the priests), faith entered into the heart of Na k iketas, who was still a boy, and he thought:
concept: Nachiketas develops faith and begins questioning the sacrifice

text: 'Unblessed 2 , surely, are the worlds to which a man goes by giving (as his promised present at a sacrifice) cows which have drunk water, eaten hay, given their milk 3 , and are barren.'
concept: Giving worthless gifts produces undesirable consequences

text: He (knowing that his father had promised to give up all that he possessed, and therefore his son also) said to his father: 'Dear father, to whom wilt thou give me?'
concept: Nachiketas asks his father to whom he will give him

text: The son said: 'I go as the first, at the head of many (who have still to die); I go in the midst of many (who are now dying). What will be the work of Yama (the ruler of the departed) which to-day he has to do unto me 2 ?
concept: Reflection on death and the fate of mortals

text: 'Look back how it was with those who came before, look forward how it will be with those who come hereafter. A mortal ripens like corn, like corn he springs up again 1 .'
concept: Human life compared to the cycle of growth and rebirth

text: 'Fire enters into the houses, when a Brâhma n a enters as a guest 2 . That fire is quenched by this peace-offering;--bring water, O Vaivasvata 3 !
concept: Proper reception of a Brahmana guest

text: 'A Brâhma n a that dwells in the house of a foolish man without receiving food to eat, destroys his hopes and expectations, his possessions, his righteousness, his sacred and his good deeds, and all his sons and cattle 4 .'
concept: Consequences of neglecting a sacred guest

text: 'O Brâhma n a, as thou, a venerable guest, hast dwelt in my house three nights without eating,
concept: Yama addresses Nachiketas after his three-night stay

text: Na k iketas said: 'O Death, as the first of the three boons I choose that Gautama, my father, be pacified, kind, and free from anger towards me; and that he may know me and greet me, when I shall have been dismissed by thee.'
concept: Nachiketas asks for reconciliation with his father as first boon

text: Yama said: 'Through my favour Auddâlaki Âru n i, thy father, will know thee, and be again towards thee as he was before. He shall sleep peacefully through the night, and free from anger, after having seen thee freed from the mouth of death.'

Na k iketas said: 'In the heaven-world there is no fear; thou art not there, O Death, and no one is afraid on account of old age. Leaving behind both hunger and thirst, and out of the reach of sorrow, all rejoice in the world of heaven.'
concept: Description of heaven as free from fear, old age and sorrow

text: 'Thou knowest, O Death, the fire-sacrifice which leads us to heaven; tell it to me, for I am full of faith. Those who live in the heaven-world reach immortality,--this I ask as my second boon.'
concept: Nachiketas asks about the fire-sacrifice leading to heaven

text: Yama said: 'I tell it thee, learn it from me, and when thou understandest that fire-sacrifice which leads to heaven, know, O Na k iketas, that it is the attainment of the endless worlds, and their firm support, hidden in darkness 1 .'
concept: Yama teaches the fire-sacrifice and its significance

text: Yama then told him that fire-sacrifice, the beginning of all the worlds 2 , and what bricks are
concept: Yama explains the structure and nature of the fire-sacrifice

text: The generous 1 , being satisfied, said to him:
concept: Yama acknowledges Nachiketas' understanding and generosity

text: 'He who has three times performed this Nâ k iketa rite, and has been united with the three (father, mother, and teacher), and has performed the three duties (study, sacrifice, almsgiving) overcomes birth and death. When he has learnt and understood this fire, which knows (or makes us know) all that is born of Brahman 3 , which is venerable and divine, then he obtains everlasting peace.'
concept: Threefold Nachiketa fire and overcoming birth and death

text: 'He who knows the three Nâ k iketa fires, and knowing the three, piles up the Nâ k iketa sacrifice, he, having first thrown off the chains of death, rejoices in the world of heaven, beyond the reach of grief.'
concept: Knowledge and performance of the three Nachiketa fires

text: 'This, O Na k iketas, is thy fire which leads to heaven, and which thou hast chosen as thy second boon. That fire all men will proclaim 4 . Choose now, O Na k iketas, thy third boon.'
concept: Yama identifies the fire as Nachiketas' second boon and asks for the third

text: Na k iketas said: 'There is that doubt, when a man is dead,--some saying, he is; others, he is not. This I should like to know, taught by thee; this is the third of my boons.'
concept: Nachiketas asks what happens to a person after death

text: Death said: 'On this point even the gods
concept: Yama acknowledges the difficulty of understanding death

text: Na k iketas said: 'On this point even the gods have doubted indeed, and thou, Death, hast declared it to be not easy to understand, and another teacher like thee is not to be found:--surely no other boon is like unto this.'
concept: Nachiketas insists on receiving knowledge of the Self after death

text: Death said: 'Choose sons and grandsons who shall live a hundred years, herds of cattle, elephants, gold, and horses. Choose the wide abode of the earth, and live thyself as many harvests as thou desirest.'
concept: Yama offers worldly wealth, children and long life instead

text: 'If you can think of any boon equal to that, choose wealth, and long life. Be (king), Na k iketas, on the wide earth 1 . I make thee the enjoyer of all desires.'
concept: Yama continues offering wealth and long life

text: 'Whatever desires are difficult to attain among mortals, ask for them according to thy wish;--these fair maidens with their chariots and musical instruments,--such are indeed not to be obtained by men,--be waited on by them whom I give to thee, but do not ask me about dying.'
concept: Yama offers pleasures and asks Nachiketas not to question death

text: Na k iketas said: 'These things last till tomorrow, O Death, for they wear out this vigour of all the senses. Even the whole of life is short. Keep thou thy horses, keep dance and song for thyself.'
concept: Nachiketas rejects temporary pleasures because they decay

text: 'No man can be made happy by wealth. Shall we possess wealth, when we see thee? Shall we live,

'What mortal, slowly decaying here below, and knowing, after having approached them, the freedom from decay enjoyed by the immortals, would delight in a long life, after he has pondered on the pleasures which arise from beauty and love 1 ?'
concept: Reflection on mortality makes worldly longevity undesirable

text: 'No, that on which there is this doubt, O Death, tell us what there is in that great Hereafter. Na k iketas does not choose another boon but that which enters into the hidden world.'
concept: Nachiketas firmly chooses knowledge of the ultimate reality after death

text: Death said: 'The good is one thing, the pleasant another; these two, having different objects, chain a man. It is well with him who clings to the good; he who chooses the pleasant, misses his end.'
concept: Distinction between the good and the pleasant

text: 'The good and the pleasant approach man: the wise goes round about them and distinguishes them. Yea, the wise prefers the good to the pleasant, but the fool chooses the pleasant through greed and avarice.'
concept: The wise choose the good while the ignorant choose the pleasant

text: 'Thou, O Na k iketas, after pondering all pleasures that are or seem delightful, hast dismissed them all. Thou hast not gone into the road 1 that leadeth to wealth, in which many men perish.'
concept: Nachiketas rejects pleasures and the path of wealth

text: 'Wide apart and leading to different points are these two, ignorance, and what is known as wisdom. I believe Na k iketas to be one who desires knowledge, for even many pleasures did not tear thee away 2 .'
concept: Wisdom and ignorance lead in completely different directions

text: 'Fools dwelling in darkness, wise in their own conceit, and puffed up with vain knowledge, go round and round, staggering to and fro, like blind men led by the blind 3 .'
concept: The ignorant, blinded by false knowledge, remain trapped in confusion

text: 'The Hereafter never rises before the eyes of the careless child, deluded by the delusion of wealth. "This is the world," he thinks, "there is no other;"--thus he falls again and again under my sway.'
concept: Attachment to wealth prevents understanding of the Hereafter

text: 'He (the Self) of whom many are not even able
concept: The Self is difficult for ordinary people to understand

text: 'That (Self), when taught by an inferior man, is not easy to be known, even though often thought upon 2 ; unless it be taught by another, there is no way to it, for it is inconceivably smaller than what is small 3 .'
concept: Knowledge of the Self requires proper teaching and cannot easily be understood through ordinary reasoning

text: 'That doctrine is not to be obtained 4 by argument, but when it is declared by another, then, O dearest, it is easy to understand. Thou hast obtained it now 5 ; thou art truly a man of true resolve. May we have always an inquirer like thee 6 !'
concept: The Self is understood through proper spiritual teaching rather than argument alone

text: Na k iketas said: 'I know that what is called a treasure is transient, for that eternal is not obtained by things which are not eternal. Hence the Nâkiketa fire(-sacrifice) has been laid by me (first); then, by means of transient things, I have obtained what is not transient (the teaching of Yama) 7 .'
concept: Nachiketas understands that eternal knowledge cannot be obtained through transient things

text: Yama said: 'Though thou hadst seen the fulfilment of all desires, the foundation of the world, the endless rewards of good deeds, the shore where
concept: Yama praises Nachiketas for rejecting worldly temptations

text: 'The wise who, by means of meditation on his Self, recognises the Ancient, who is difficult to be seen, who has entered into the dark, who is hidden in the cave, who dwells in the abyss, as God, he indeed leaves joy and sorrow far behind 2 .'
concept: Meditation on the Self leads beyond joy and sorrow

text: 'A mortal who has heard this and embraced it, who has separated from it all qualities, and has thus reached the subtle Being, rejoices, because he has obtained what is a cause for rejoicing. The house (of Brahman) is open, I believe, O Na k iketas.'
concept: One who understands the subtle Self attains a state worthy of rejoicing

text: Na k iketas said: 'That which thou seest as neither this nor that, as neither effect nor cause, as neither past nor future, tell me that.'
concept: Nachiketas asks Yama to describe the reality beyond ordinary categories of cause, effect, past and future

text: Yama said: 'That word (or place) which all the Vedas record, which all penances proclaim, which men desire when they live as religious students, that word I tell thee briefly, it is Om 3 .'
concept: Yama identifies Om as the supreme reality indicated by the Vedas

text: 'That (imperishable) syllable means Brahman, that syllable means the highest (Brahman); he who knows that syllable, whatever he desires, is his.'
concept: Om represents the imperishable Brahman and the highest reality

text: 'This is the best support, this is the highest support; he who knows that support is magnified in the world of Brahmâ.'
concept: Knowledge of the imperishable Om provides the highest spiritual support

text: 'The knowing (Self) is not born, it dies not; it sprang from nothing, nothing sprang from it. The
concept: The Self is unborn, eternal and beyond ordinary birth and death

text: 'If the killer thinks that he kills, if the killed thinks that he is killed, they do not understand; for this one does not kill, nor is that one killed.'
concept: The true Self neither kills nor is killed

text: 'The Self 2 , smaller than small, greater than great, is hidden in the heart of that creature. A man who is free from desires and free from grief, sees the majesty of the Self by the grace of the Creator 3 .'
concept: The Self is simultaneously smaller than the smallest and greater than the greatest

text: 'Though sitting still, he walks far; though lying down, he goes everywhere 4 . Who, save myself, is able to know that God who rejoices and rejoices not?'
concept: The Self transcends ordinary ideas of movement and activity

text: 'The wise who knows the Self as bodiless within the bodies, as unchanging among changing things, as great and omnipresent, does never grieve.'
concept: The wise person recognises the unchanging Self within changing bodies

text: 'That Self 5 cannot be gained by the Veda, nor by understanding, nor by much learning. He whom the Self chooses, by him the Self can be gained. The Self chooses him (his body) as his own.'
concept: The Self cannot be attained merely through scripture, intellect or extensive learning

text: 'But he who has not first turned away from his wickedness, who is not tranquil, and subdued, or whose mind is not at rest, he can never obtain the Self (even) by knowledge!
concept: Moral purity, tranquillity and control of the mind are necessary for attaining the Self

text: 'Who then knows where He is, He to whom the Brahmans and Kshatriyas are (as it were) but food 6 , and death itself a condiment?'
concept: The ultimate Self is beyond even death and worldly categories

text: 'There are the two 1 , drinking their reward in the world of their own works, entered into the cave (of the heart), dwelling on the highest summit (the ether in the heart). Those who know Brahman call them shade and light; likewise, those householders who perform the Tri n â k iketa sacrifice.'
concept: Two principles dwell in the heart and experience the results of action

text: 'May we be able to master that Nâ k iketa rite which is a bridge for sacrificers; also that which is the highest, imperishable Brahman for those who wish to cross over to the fearless shore 2 .'
concept: The Nachiketa fire and Brahman are presented as means of crossing beyond fear

text: 'Know the Self to be sitting in the chariot, the body to be the chariot, the intellect (buddhi) the charioteer, and the mind the reins 3 .'
concept: The chariot metaphor identifies the Self, body, intellect and mind

text: 'The senses they call the horses, the objects of the senses their roads. When he (the Highest Self) is in union with the body, the senses, and the mind, then wise people call him the Enjoyer.'
concept: Senses are compared to horses and sense objects to their paths

text: 'He who has no understanding and whose mind
concept: Lack of understanding and uncontrolled mind lead to poor control of the senses

text: 'But he who has understanding and whose mind is always firmly held, his senses are under control, like good horses of a charioteer.'
concept: A disciplined intellect and controlled mind keep the senses under control

text: 'He who has no understanding, who is unmindful and always impure, never reaches that place, but enters into the round of births.'
concept: An uncontrolled and impure person remains trapped in rebirth

text: 'But he who has understanding, who is mindful and always pure, reaches indeed that place, from whence he is not born again.'
concept: A mindful and pure person reaches the state beyond rebirth

text: 'But he who has understanding for his charioteer, and who holds the reins of the mind, he reaches the end of his journey, and that is the highest place of Vish n u.'
concept: Proper control of intellect and mind leads to the highest state

text: 'Beyond the senses there are the objects, beyond the objects there is the mind, beyond the mind there is the intellect, the Great Self is beyond the intellect.'
concept: Reality is presented as a hierarchy from senses to objects, mind, intellect and the Great Self

text: 'Beyond the Great there is the Undeveloped, beyond the Undeveloped there is the Person (purusha). Beyond the Person there is nothing--this is the goal, the highest road.'
concept: The Supreme Person lies beyond the Great and the Unmanifest and is the ultimate goal

text: 'That Self is hidden in all beings and does not shine forth, but it is seen by subtle seers through their sharp and subtle intellect.'
concept: The Self is hidden within all beings and perceived by subtle intellect

text: 'A wise man should keep down speech and mind 1 ; he should keep them within the Self which is knowledge; he should keep knowledge within the Self which is the Great; and he should keep that (the Great) within the Self which is the Quiet.'
concept: A practitioner should progressively withdraw speech, mind, knowledge and intellect into the deeper Self

text: 'Rise, awake! having obtained your boons 2 ,
concept: The seeker is urged to rise, awaken and pursue higher knowledge

text: 'He who has perceived that which is without sound, without touch, without form, without decay, without taste, eternal, without smell, without beginning, without end, beyond the Great, and unchangeable, is freed from the jaws of death.'
concept: Realisation of the transcendent, imperishable reality frees one from death

text: 'A wise man who has repeated or heard the ancient story of Na k iketas told by Death, is magnified in the world of Brahman.'
concept: Hearing and understanding the teaching of Nachiketas leads to spiritual merit

text: 'And he who repeats this greatest mystery in an assembly of Brâhmans, or full of devotion at the time of the S râddha sacrifice, obtains thereby infinite rewards.'
concept: Reciting and teaching this spiritual mystery is associated with spiritual rewards

text: Death said: 'The Self-existent pierced the openings (of the senses) so that they turn forward: therefore man looks forward, not backward into himself. Some wise man, however, with his eyes closed and wishing for immortality, saw the Self behind.'
concept: Human senses naturally turn outward, while the wise turn inward to perceive the Self

text: 'Children follow after outward pleasures, and fall into the snare of wide-spread death. Wise men only, knowing the nature of what is immortal, do not look for anything stable here among things unstable.'
concept: Ordinary people pursue external pleasures while the wise seek the immortal

text: 'That by which we know form, taste, smell, sounds, and loving touches, by that also we know what exists besides. This is that (which thou hast asked for).'
concept: The faculty through which objects are perceived also reveals deeper existence

text: 'The wise, when he knows that that by which he perceives all objects in sleep or in waking is the great omnipresent Self, grieves no more.'
concept: The Self is the consciousness underlying both waking and sleep

text: 'He who knows this living soul which eats honey (perceives objects) as being the Self, always near, the Lord of the past and the future, henceforward fears no more. This is that.'
concept: Knowing the Self removes fear and reveals its timeless nature

text: 'He who (knows) him 1 who was born first from
concept: The Self is described through its primordial and cosmic nature

text: '(He who knows) Aditi also, who is one with all deities, who arises with Prâ n a (breath or Hira n yagarbha), who, entering into the heart, abides therein, and was born from the elements. This is that.'
concept: Aditi and Prana are connected with the universal Self dwelling within the heart

text: 'There is Agni (fire), the all-seeing, hidden in the two fire-sticks, well-guarded like a child (in the womb) by the mother, day after day to be adored by men when they awake and bring oblations. This is that.'
concept: Agni hidden within the fire-sticks symbolises a concealed divine principle

text: 'And that whence the sun rises, and whither it goes to set, there all the Devas are contained, and no one goes beyond. This is that 2 .'
concept: The divine reality encompasses the entire cosmic order

text: 'What is here (visible in the world), the same is there (invisible in Brahman); and what is there, the same is here. He who sees any difference here (between Brahman and the world), goes from death to death.'
concept: The visible world and Brahman are fundamentally connected; seeing separation leads to repeated death

text: 'Even by the mind this (Brahman) is to be obtained, and then there is no difference whatsoever. He goes from death to death who sees any difference here.'
concept: Brahman is realised through the mind, and perceiving difference perpetuates bondage

text: 'The person (purusha), of the size of a thumb 3 , stands in the middle of the Self (body?), as lord of the past and the future, and henceforward fears no more. This is that.'
'That person, of the size of a thumb, is like a light without smoke, lord of the past and the future, he is the same to-day and to-morrow. This is that.'
'As rain-water that has fallen on a mountain-ridge runs down the rocks on all sides, thus does he, who sees a difference between qualities, run after them on all sides.'
'As pure water poured into pure water remains the same, thus, O Gautama, is the Self of a thinker who knows.'

'There is a town with eleven 1 gates belonging to the Unborn (Brahman), whose thoughts are never crooked. He who approaches it, grieves no more, and liberated (from all bonds of ignorance) becomes free. This is that.'

'He (Brahman) 2 is the swan (sun), dwelling in the bright heaven; he is the Vasu (air), dwelling in the sky; he is the sacrificer (fire), dwelling on the hearth; he is the guest (Soma), dwelling in the sacrificial jar; he dwells in men, in gods (vara), in the sacrifice ( ri ta), in heaven; he is born in the water, on earth, in the sacrifice ( ri ta), on the mountains; he is the True and the Great.'
'He (Brahman) it is who sends up the breath (prâ n a), and who throws back the breath (apâna). All the Devas (senses) worship him, the adorable (or the dwarf), who sits in the centre.'
'When that incorporated (Brahman), who dwells in the body, is torn away and freed from the body, what remains then? This is that.'
'No mortal lives by the breath that goes up and by the breath that goes down. We live by another, in whom these two repose.'
'Well then, O Gautama, I shall tell thee this mystery, the old Brahman, and what happens to the Self, after reaching death.'
'Some enter the womb in order to have a body, as organic beings, others go into inorganic matter, according to their work and according to their knowledge 1 .'
